_note: Section 7 drafts by reader 70 (nicotine replacement, vapes and pouches for stopping smoking; Cochrane reviews), for a targeted second reading

tasks.locator: Summary of findings, Table 1; Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Any form of NRT against placebo or no NRT, abstinence at 6 months or longer (follow-up 6 to 24 months): RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.49 to 1.61), fixed-effect, I² 39%, 133 comparisons from 131 trials, 64,640 participants. The table assumes 105 per 1,000 without NRT and gives 162 per 1,000 (156 to 168) with NRT, a difference of 57 per 1,000 (editors' subtraction: about 6 in 100). The authors rate the evidence high certainty (GRADE).

tasks.locator: Summary of findings, Table 1 (limited and intensive behavioural support rows)
tasks.extracted: Limited behavioural support: 40 per 1,000 without NRT against 62 per 1,000 (60 to 64) with NRT; intensive behavioural support: 150 against 232 per 1,000 (224 to 242). Editors' subtraction: about 2 and about 8 more people in 100.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, table after the 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1
tasks.extracted: RR by product (comparisons; participants): gum 1.49 (1.40 to 1.60; 56; 22,581; I² 40%); patch 1.64 (1.53 to 1.75; 51; 25,754; I² 24%); tablets or lozenges 1.52 (1.32 to 1.74; 8; 4,439; I² 71%); inhalator 1.90 (1.36 to 2.67; 4; 976); intranasal spray 2.02 (1.49 to 2.73; 4; 887); oral spray 2.48 (1.24 to 4.94; 1 trial; 479); choice of product 1.37 (1.25 to 1.52; 7; 8,288). Product estimates are subgroups of trials each against its own control group, not head-to-head comparisons.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The I² of 71% in the lozenge or tablet subgroup is driven by one new trial (RR 1.08). Twelve trials had lower quit rates with NRT than control (every interval included no difference) and in a further 73% of trials the interval included no difference. One large patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease found 14% against 11% quit at 6 months and 10% against 12% at 48 weeks.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to risk of bias and study methods
tasks.extracted: Sensitivity analyses: excluding high-risk trials RR 1.61 (1.52 to 1.69); only the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37 to 1.71); excluding trials without biochemical validation 1.62 (1.55 to 1.70); placebo-controlled trials only 1.61 (1.53 to 1.70).

tasks.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 6th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: 12 trials low risk of bias in all domains and 36 high risk in at least one; adequate allocation concealment reported in 39 trials (29%); 43 trials had no matched placebo; 117 trials validated abstinence biochemically; follow-up was only 6 months in 15 gum, 19 patch, 4 combination and 1 lozenge trial.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to treatment settings, 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 4
tasks.extracted: By setting: antenatal clinics RR 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62; 4 trials; 1,675 participants), the only setting without a statistically significant effect; the other settings 1.39 (hospitals) to 1.70 (smoking clinics).

tasks.locator: Discussion › Trials in special populations, 1st paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Two small adolescent trials (Moolchan 2005; Scherphof 2014) did not detect an effect on quitting at 6 months or longer; the authors say there is little evidence on NRT in people smoking fewer than 10 to 15 cigarettes a day.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence base, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1 footnotes 1 and 2
tasks.extracted: Authors: unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing; the funnel plot shows some asymmetry; a cited meta-analysis (Etter 2007) found pharmaceutical-funded gum and patch trials had slightly higher effect sizes; the magnitude of effectiveness may be smaller than estimated. The table footnotes give the reasons for not downgrading: restricting to low-risk trials did not alter the effect, and with so many trials the asymmetry does not suggest that adding smaller trials with lower risk ratios would change the results significantly.
tasks.quote: the magnitude of the effectiveness of NRT may be smaller than our estimates suggest

tasks.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Notes of each study (editors' count)
tasks.extracted: Editors' count of the 136 included entries: about 80 name a drug company as funder, co-funder or supplier of study product, about 40 name only government, charity or university funders, about 15 report no source. The review did not analyse results by funder. Approximate: some entries are two halves of one trial and some company links are product supply only.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1; Analysis 4.1
tasks.extracted: Combination NRT (patch plus a fast-acting form) against single-form NRT, abstinence at 6 months or longer: RR 1.27 (1.17 to 1.37), I² 12%, 16 studies, 12,169 participants; 137 per 1,000 with a single form against 174 per 1,000 (160 to 187) with combination (editors' subtraction: about 4 in 100). The authors rate it high certainty; the estimate was unchanged without the high-risk trials.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 1st paragraph; Analysis 4.1.1 to 4.1.3; Characteristics of included studies › Dignan 2019
tasks.extracted: Subgroups: against patch alone RR 1.24 (1.13 to 1.37), I² 28%, 13 studies, 9,552 participants (the text prints 9,522; the table's subgroups sum to the pool's 12,169); against a fast-acting form alone 1.30 (1.09 to 1.54), I² 0%, 6 studies, 2,364; against a choice of a single form 5.16 (1.18 to 22.59), 1 study, 253 (Dignan 2019, high risk of bias because most participants were lost to follow-up). No clear subgroup difference (I² 45.8%, P = 0.16).

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 (as described in the text)
tasks.extracted: The funnel plot for the 16 combination studies, the only comparison with 10 or more studies, gave no evidence of publication bias, which the authors say should be read with caution because the number of studies is small.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Fast-acting NRT versus patch, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 5; Analysis 6.1
tasks.extracted: Fast-acting NRT against the nicotine patch, abstinence at 6 months or longer: RR 0.90 (0.77 to 1.05), I² 0%, 8 studies, 3,319 participants; 164 per 1,000 with the patch against 148 per 1,000 (126 to 172) with a fast-acting form (editors' subtraction: about 2 fewer in 100, interval 4 fewer to 1 more). By form: inhaler 0.59 (0.22 to 1.60; 1 study; 222), nasal spray 0.90 (0.64 to 1.27; 2; 1,272), lozenge 0.94 (0.79 to 1.12; 3; 1,707), gum 0.58 (0.26 to 1.31; 2; 118). The authors rate it high certainty; no subgroup difference (P = 0.57). The overall effect was not sensitive to removing high-risk studies or, post hoc, Moolchan 2005, a trial in adolescents.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice
tasks.extracted: The authors limit generalisation to adults motivated to quit who smoke about 20 or more cigarettes a day (highest mean 38) and say there is little evidence for people smoking fewer than 15 a day; e-cigarettes are not covered; unpublished data may be missing; reference lists were not screened uniformly across versions.

tasks.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Certainty of the evidence, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Tables 1 and 5 footnotes
tasks.extracted: Of 68 trials, 9 low risk of bias in every domain, 28 high in at least one, 31 unclear. Removing high-risk trials changed the interpretation only for preloading (outside this claim); the footnotes to the combination and fast-acting-against-patch rows say that restricting to low-risk studies gave a consistent estimate and confidence interval.

tasks.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Notes of each study (editors' count); Discussion › Certainty of the evidence, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Editors' count of the 68 trials: 38 name a manufacturer as funder, sponsor, supplier of product or employer of authors (20 as funder or sponsor); 23 name none; 7 report no source. Of the 16 combination trials 9 involve a manufacturer (4 funded or sponsored by Pharmacia or employing its staff, 5 through product supply or affiliation) and 7 do not; of the 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials 6 do, 1 names none and 1 reports no source. The review states that it did not assess bias from industry funding, judging it less applicable to comparisons between ways of using NRT.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Patch therapy › Dose and Duration; Fast-acting NRT › Gum dose; NRT preloading versus standard post-quit use; Summary of findings, Tables 2, 3, 4 and 7
tasks.extracted: Comparisons outside this claim, held on the study card: a higher against a lower patch dose favoured the higher dose in two of three comparisons (moderate certainty); 4 mg against 2 mg gum favoured the higher strength overall but only in a post hoc higher-dependence subgroup; starting before the quit date favoured early use (RR 1.25) but not once high-risk trials were removed (1.16); no clear difference for patch duration, combination duration, tapering, fixed against as-needed use, gum duration or free against purchased NRT, mostly from one or two small trials.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 6
tasks.extracted: Chest pain or palpitations: odds ratio 1.88 (1.37 to 2.57), 15 included and excluded trials in which they were reported, 11,074 participants, with 2.5% of NRT groups and 1.4% of control groups affected (editors' subtraction: about 1 more in 100). An earlier meta-analysis (Mills 2010) found OR 2.06 (1.51 to 2.82) in 12 studies. The authors call the events extremely rare and report no evidence of an excess of serious cardiac problems.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Appendix 3
tasks.extracted: Adverse events were not pooled, because the nature, timing and duration of symptoms were reported too variably; they are tabulated by trial in Appendix 3. Local effects listed: gum, hiccups, gastrointestinal disturbance, jaw pain, orodental problems; patch, skin sensitivity and irritation (up to 54% of people in one cited source, usually mild); inhalator and nasal and oral sprays, irritation at the site of use (throat irritation, coughing, oral burning; nasal irritation and runny nose; hiccups); sublingual tablets, hiccups, burning in the mouth, sore throat, cough, dry lips, mouth ulcers. Adolescents reported similar events to adults.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Adverse events, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: In one patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease (Joseph 1996) serious adverse events were not more common with the patch, and cardiovascular events such as worse angina (about 16% of participants) did not differ by arm. Six trials in pregnant women did not detect significant increases in serious adverse events. A network meta-analysis the review cites (Mills 2014) found more cardiovascular events with NRT overall, driven by lower-level events; its figures are quoted from another review and were not checked.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Summary of findings, Table 1; Appendix 2
tasks.extracted: Combination against single form: serious adverse events RR 4.44 (0.76 to 25.85), 5 studies, 2,888 participants, seven events in total, 1 against 3 per 1,000 (1 to 18), low certainty (two levels for imprecision); any cardiac event RR 0.66 (0.22 to 2.05; 2 studies; 656); withdrawals due to treatment RR 1.12 (0.57 to 2.20; 5 studies; 3,070; I² 73%), 12 against 14 per 1,000, very low certainty. Only 3 of the 16 combination trials reported cardiac events; Piper 2009 (1,504 participants) reported 32 serious events not split by arm.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Fast-acting NRT versus patch, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Summary of findings, Table 5
tasks.extracted: Fast-acting forms against the patch: withdrawals due to treatment RR 4.23 (1.54 to 11.63), 3 studies, 1,482 participants, 5 against 23 per 1,000 (8 to 63), very low certainty; nasal spray against patch RR 3.47 (1.15 to 10.46), 1 study, 922, 3.0% against 0.9%. Serious events: three of four studies (1,252 participants) had none; the fourth RR 1.75 (0.52 to 5.92; 642 participants); very low certainty. Cardiac events reported by arm in one small trial: none in either arm.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice
tasks.extracted: The authors state that evidence for the safety and tolerability of different ways of using NRT is limited, that many comparisons rest on sparse studies and that further research could strengthen or change the findings.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Direct comparisons between nicotine EC and other pharmacotherapies › Cessation, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings 1
tasks.extracted: Nicotine vape against NRT, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.61 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.12), I² 55%, 11 trials, 4,114 participants. Summary of findings: 6 per 100 with NRT (an assumed quit rate with limited behavioural support) against 10 per 100 (7 to 13) with a nicotine vape, about 4 more in 100 (interval 1 to 7 more; editors' subtraction). The review rates this high certainty with no downgrade. Six of the 11 trials were at low risk of bias, three unclear and two high.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Subgroup and sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (rows Analysis 1.1 and 1.2)
tasks.extracted: NRT comparison: the pregnancy trial did not differ from the rest (P = 0.89). Split by NRT type (4 trials combination NRT, 5 single-form, 2 unclear) there was little evidence of a subgroup difference (P = 0.11, I² 55.1%; P = 0.52 comparing combination with single-form only). Without the one industry-funded trial (Russell 2021) RR 1.72 (1.23 to 2.39), I² 56%; without the two high-risk trials RR 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34), I² 55%. For the combination-NRT subgroup Table 2 gives RR 1.95 (1.01 to 3.73), I² 74%, after removing high-risk trials; the main-analysis subgroup estimates are in a forest plot that was not read.

tasks.locator: Results › Reporting biases; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Synthesis methods
tasks.extracted: Six pools had 10 or more studies and five showed some asymmetry, including the NRT cessation pool (11 trials) and the behavioural-support cessation pool (11 trials). The authors say plots with this few studies are not diagnostic, that asymmetry could reflect unpublished small trials that showed no benefit or differences between trials, that they did not downgrade for publication bias and will keep monitoring. The Methods define I² above 50% as substantial; the NRT cessation pool has 55% and was not downgraded for inconsistency, while adverse events in the same comparison (72%) were.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Versus non-nicotine, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Analysis 8.1); Summary of findings 2
tasks.extracted: Nicotine vape against non-nicotine vape, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.34 (1.05 to 1.69), I² 0%, 7 trials (five cartridge, two refillable), 1,918 participants; 6 per 100 (assumed) against 8 per 100 (6 to 10), about 2 more in 100 (interval 0 to 4; editors' subtraction). Moderate certainty: not downgraded for risk of bias (one high-risk trial; without it RR 1.40, 1.09 to 1.81), one level for imprecision (fewer than 300 quits). Without the one industry-funded trial (Caponnetto 2013) RR 1.28 (1.01 to 1.64).

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Study product use; Long-term nicotine EC and combustible cigarette use
tasks.extracted: Against NRT: use of the allocated product at six months or longer was reported by 5 trials (none at high risk of bias; one, Russell 2021, industry-funded) and could not be pooled (I² 95%); in 3 more people in the vape arm kept using it than in the NRT arm, in 2 (Russell 2021, Lee 2018) there was no difference. Five trials (counted separately in the text: none industry-funded, one high risk) reported long-term product patterns: vaping without smoking RR 4.40 (1.27 to 15.28), I² 78%, 2,776 participants; abstinence from both vaping and smoking RR 0.49 (0.26 to 0.91), I² 31%, 2,776; concurrent vaping and smoking higher in the vape arm in 3 of 4 trials (not pooled); smoking without vaping RR 0.76 (0.58 to 1.01), I² 83%, 4 trials, 2,543. Absolute counts are in forest plots that were not read.

tasks.locator: Results › Description of studies › Funding; Declarations of interest; Table 1; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Funding of the 80 trials: 8 report tobacco or vaping industry support (Caponnetto 2013 and 2023, Cravo 2016, Edmiston 2022, Kanobe 2022, Rose 2023, Russell 2021, Xu 2023), 66 report none, 6 do not report. One industry-funded trial sits in each of the three cessation pools (Russell 2021 in the NRT pool, Caponnetto 2013 in the non-nicotine pool, Xu 2023 in the behavioural-support pool); removing it left each estimate positive. The review's funding comes from Cancer Research UK, NIHR infrastructure funding and, for some new outcomes, the US National Cancer Institute and FDA Center for Tobacco Products; the authors state they receive no tobacco or vaping industry funding. Six review authors are authors of included trials and state they took no part in eligibility, extraction, risk of bias or GRADE decisions for those trials.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Limitations of the review processes; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice and for research
tasks.extracted: Authors: imprecision remains the main limit; longer-term health effects are unknown and the review includes safety data to two years only; the trials tested regulated nicotine vapes, and illicit or THC-containing products may have different harm profiles; the field and devices change quickly and trial devices lag the market; planned subgroups by device type could not be run; unpublished data may be missing; the search ran to 1 January 2026; all trials were in adults.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Cessation › Versus behavioural support or no support, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2 (Analysis 9.1); Summary of findings 3
tasks.extracted: Nicotine vape against behavioural support only or no support, abstinence at six months or longer: RR 1.75 (1.39 to 2.20), I² 13%, 11 trials (five refillable, three cartridge, three pod), 7,214 participants; 5 per 100 (assumed) against 9 per 100 (7 to 11), about 4 more in 100 (interval 2 to 6; editors' subtraction). Low certainty: two levels for risk of bias because blinding was not possible and the vape arm received more support. One trial was industry-funded (Xu 2023, JUUL Labs); without it RR 1.53 (1.30 to 1.79). One trial (Pulvers 2020) could not be pooled.

tasks.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies; Summary of findings 3 footnote a; Results › Reporting biases
tasks.extracted: Across the 80 trials (RoB 1): 12 low risk of bias, 27 unclear, 41 high; performance bias high in 24. The summary-of-findings footnote gives lack of blinding and differential support between arms as the reason for the two-level downgrade. The funnel plot for the behavioural-support cessation pool (11 trials) shows some asymmetry; the authors say plots with this few studies are not diagnostic and did not downgrade for publication bias.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Advice to use EC to stop smoking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Advice to use a vape without being given one, against no such advice: RR 1.02 (0.88 to 1.19), I² 0%, 2 trials (Martinez 2021, low risk of bias, in people who already vaped; Elling 2023, high risk), 2,652 participants; no clear difference, unchanged without Elling 2023. A third trial (Vickerman 2022, 52 participants) found more adverse events with the advice (RR 1.27, 0.72 to 2.26) and no serious events. None industry-funded.

tasks.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice and for research
tasks.extracted: Authors: longer-term health effects are unknown and the review includes safety data to two years only; the trials tested regulated nicotine vapes; unpublished data may be missing; all trials were in adults; the search ran to 1 January 2026.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events, 1st paragraph and Sensitivity analyses; Serious adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Narrative summary of unpooled studies; Summary of findings 1
tasks.extracted: Nicotine vape against NRT: any adverse event RR 0.95 (0.72 to 1.24), I² 72%, 8 trials, 3,107 participants, 41 per 100 with NRT against 39 per 100 (30 to 51) with the vape, low certainty (imprecision and inconsistency). Serious events RD 0.01 (−0.01 to 0.02), I² 0%, 10 trials, 4,045, 6 per 100 against 7 per 100 (5 to 8), moderate certainty (fewer than 300 events). No trial in either pool was industry-funded. Unpooled: Hajek 2019 found nausea more often with NRT and throat or mouth irritation more often with the vape.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events › Versus non-nicotine; Serious adverse events › Versus non-nicotine EC; Summary of findings 2; Table 2 (Analyses 8.2 and 8.3)
tasks.extracted: Nicotine against non-nicotine vape: any adverse event RR 1.01 (0.95 to 1.08), I² 0%, 6 trials, 909 participants, 46 against 46 per 100 (44 to 50), moderate certainty (imprecision). Serious events RD 0.00 (−0.01 to 0.01), I² 0%, 11 trials, 1,786, 2 against 2 per 100 (1 to 3), low certainty (fewer than 100 events, two levels); five of 12 trials reporting serious events had none. Two unpooled trials found similar adverse event rates, two reported more events with the nicotine vape. Industry funding: one trial in the any-adverse-event pool and two (Caponnetto 2013, Rose 2023) in the serious-event pool; removing them made no change to either result (Table 2: RR 1.01, 0.95 to 1.08; RD −0.00, −0.01 to 0.01).

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events › Versus behavioural support or no support; Narrative summary of unpooled studies; Serious adverse events › Versus behavioural support or no support; Summary of findings 3; Table 2 (Analysis 9.2)
tasks.extracted: Nicotine vape against behavioural support only or no support: any adverse event RR 1.22 (1.00 to 1.49), I² 58%, 11 trials, 2,801 participants, 43 against 52 per 100 (43 to 64), very low certainty (risk of bias and imprecision). Serious events RD 0.00 (−0.00 to 0.01), I² 0%, 18 trials, 5,032, 3 against 3 per 100 (3 to 4), very low certainty; ten of 18 trials reported none. Twelve further trials gave adverse event data that could not be pooled, with mixed direction by symptom (more throat irritation, cough and dry mouth in vape arms of some trials, fewer respiratory symptoms in others). Industry support: one trial (Cravo 2016) in the any-adverse-event pool and two (Edmiston 2022, Cravo 2016) in the serious-event pool; the review says removing them did not affect interpretation (Table 2 gives RR 1.26, 0.96 to 1.66, I² 60%, for any adverse event without the industry-supported trial).

tasks.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice and for research
tasks.extracted: Authors: longer-term health effects are unknown and the review includes safety data to two years only; the trials tested regulated nicotine vapes and illicit or THC-containing products may have different harm profiles; imprecision remains the main limit; unpublished data may be missing.

tasks.locator: Results › Included studies, Table 4 (overview), Participants, Interventions and comparators; Results of the search
tasks.extracted: Four randomised trials, 284 participants: Avila 2024 (USA, 45 people: pouch, e-cigarette, no intervention); Caldwell 2010 (New Zealand, 63, cross-over of pouch, snus and nicotine gum, adverse events only); NCT04250727 (USA, 30: higher against lower strength, registry record only); Rensch 2023 (USA, 146, tobacco-industry funded: pouches of three strengths against a no-tobacco group and a continue-smoking group). All enrolled adults who smoked; three enrolled people not planning to quit; follow-up 7 days to 8 weeks. Ten ongoing trials are listed.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary of findings 1, row 1 and footnotes a and b
tasks.extracted: Pouch against minimal control, abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 given pouches had quit against 0 of 9 with no intervention; RR 1.58 (0.07 to 35.32), 1 trial, 27 participants (Avila 2024, high risk of bias); very low certainty (two levels for risk of bias and two for imprecision). The table's 11 per 1,000 and 18 per 1,000 come from a zero-event correction, not observed rates. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking at week 8: mean difference −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58), 19 people with complete data.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus e-cigarettes › Smoking behaviour and Biomarkers; Summary of findings 3
tasks.extracted: Pouch against e-cigarette (nicotine pods), abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 quit with pouches against 4 of 18 with e-cigarettes; RR 0.25 (0.03 to 2.02), 1 trial, 36 participants; the table gives 222 per 1,000 with e-cigarettes against 56 per 1,000 (7 to 449) with pouches (editors' subtraction: about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate). Low certainty (two levels for imprecision; 5 events in all); not downgraded for risk of bias because both arms were equally intensive although unblinded. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: MD 5.32 (−2.16 to 12.80), 26 people with complete data; exhaled carbon monoxide higher with pouches, interval including no difference.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Smoking behaviour and Adverse events; Table 5 (NCT04250727)
tasks.extracted: Higher against lower strength pouch (NCT04250727; registry record, unclear risk of bias), abstinence at week 4: 2 of 15 quit at the higher strength against 0 of 15 at the lower; RR 5.00 (0.26 to 96.13), 30 participants; certainty not assessed (a dose comparison was not a planned summary-of-findings comparison). Cigarettes per day (log scale) lower with the higher strength: MD −0.20 (−0.27 to −0.13), n = 30. Any adverse event 13 of 15 in each arm; two participants in the higher-strength arm reported nicotine toxicity symptoms during dual use of cigarettes and pouches.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events (ONP against minimal control; ONP versus e-cigarettes; ONP at different doses); Summary of findings 1 and 3; Plain language summary › What did we find?
tasks.extracted: Serious adverse events: none in any arm in the trials reporting them. Against minimal control, 2 trials (Avila 2024; Rensch 2023), 124 participants, very low certainty (two levels for risk of bias, two for imprecision); against e-cigarettes, 1 trial, 26 participants, low certainty (imprecision); higher against lower strength, NCT04250727 and Rensch 2023, 77 participants; Rensch 2023 against a no-tobacco group, none. Follow-up 1 to 8 weeks. The authors conclude it is unclear whether pouches change the chance of a serious event.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events; ONP versus snus; ONP versus nicotine replacement therapy; Table 5
tasks.extracted: Other adverse events (not pooled): cough and shortness of breath were more frequent with pouches than with e-cigarettes in the first week of Avila 2024 (cough 5 against 3, breathlessness 6 against 1 people) and similar by week 4; Rensch 2023 reported 86 events in 56 of 146 people (38%), 76 mild and 10 moderate, headache most frequent, 4 judged related to the product, not split by arm; Caldwell 2010 (63 people, cross-over, rating scales) found side effects uncommon for pouch, snus and gum, with fewer reports of bad taste with pouches than with snus or gum.

tasks.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Biomarkers; ONP versus no tobacco or nicotine product use › Biomarkers; Summary of findings 1, rows 3 and 4
tasks.extracted: Biomarkers against minimal control (Rensch 2023, tobacco-industry funded, high risk of bias, 53 people, about one week): NNAL mean difference −265.30 ng/g creatinine (−350.64 to −179.96) from a control mean of 330; COHb −6.7% (−8.33 to −5.07) from a control mean of 11.3%; 16 further urinary biomarkers all favoured pouches with intervals excluding no difference. Very low certainty (risk of bias, imprecision). Against a no-tobacco group (46 people) none of 18 biomarkers clearly differed. Avila 2024 (19 people) found lower exhaled carbon monoxide with pouches than continued smoking, interval including no difference.

tasks.locator: Results › Description of studies › Outcomes; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Authors' conclusions
tasks.extracted: Gaps stated by the review: no study of prevalence of smoking or other nicotine use; no data on pouches for stopping or cutting down vaping, heated tobacco, snus or other products (all participants smoked); no data on metals or inflammatory markers; no trial with follow-up beyond 8 weeks; no abstinence result for the comparison with nicotine replacement; at most two studies in any analysis, so serious imprecision for every outcome; ten ongoing studies; industry reports were not searched; evidence reaches January 2025.

tasks.locator: Results › Included studies › Funding; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 2nd paragraph; Sources of support; Declarations of interest
tasks.extracted: Rensch 2023 was funded by the pouch manufacturer (a tobacco company); the other three trials by philanthropic, academic or governmental bodies. The industry trial reported no smoking outcome, no serious events, and the largest set of biomarker results. The review was funded by the US National Cancer Institute and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products through CAsToR 3.0; the review says no author took part in an included trial; no author declares funding from a tobacco, pouch or e-cigarette company (some declare payments from smoking-cessation medicine makers and public bodies).

tasks.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 7th paragraphs
